fieldData.name: Fertiliser Finance in Africa: Trade Credit, Farm Affordability and Soil Health
fieldData.standfirst: A guarantee can get fertiliser into a dealer's warehouse. It cannot tell a farmer whether the input will arrive before planting, suit the field or pay for itself at harvest. The investment case for fertiliser finance turns on the distance between those two decisions. Evidence from Kenya, Tanzania and Sierra Leone shows how funders can make that distance visible before they expand a facility.
fieldData.subtitle: Evidence from Kenya, Tanzania and Sierra Leone on how guarantees can translate into timely, suitable and financially viable farm inputs
fieldData.hero-caption: StoneComms editorial illustration: farm input distribution and soil advice meet at the edge of a field. Conceptual scene.
fieldData.hero-alt-text: A farmer shows soil to an agricultural adviser beside crop rows, with a worker moving sacks on a handcart behind them.
fieldData.article-body:
EXECUTIVE THESIS

  • Measure success at the point of farm use as well as at the point of trade credit.
  • Separate the risks of stocking a dealer, lending to a household and selecting an input for a particular field.
  • Expand guarantees only where matched evidence shows timely delivery, a viable farm proposition and appropriate nutrient management.

StoneComms original synthesis: The decision to guarantee trade credit should be tested against two linked records. A channel ledger tracks who received credit, what stock reached dealers and on what terms. A farm ledger tracks what farmers actually paid, when the input arrived, whether it suited the field and what happened to margins and repayment. These ledgers serve different purposes; together they show where the financing mechanism stopped working.

The cases identify different ways to connect those records. They do not establish that one country or delivery partner outperforms another. The paper proposes appraisal and measurement conditions for funders, lenders and implementers, using programme documents and a clearly bounded research example.

WHY THE QUESTION MATTERS NOW

The African Development Bank's Africa Fertilizer Financing Mechanism (AFFM) published its 2025 annual report on 2 October 2026. It reported that supported projects facilitated access to 41,164 tonnes of fertiliser and that US$12.3 million in trade credit guarantees helped support US$28.7 million in fertiliser sales during the reporting year. It also reported 4,523 soil tests and approvals of new projects in Kenya and Sierra Leone. These are programme figures; they do not show which farmers received advice or used an input that improved their margins. [1]

The World Bank's October 2026 outlook projected an annual increase of about 14 per cent in its global fertiliser price index for 2026. Its November food-security update reported that the index rose in October, with individual nutrients moving in different directions. A global index can inform a downside scenario. It is neither a local shop price nor a forecast of the costs facing a particular farmer. [2,3]

Guarantees become especially attractive when higher input prices make the same stock more expensive to finance. That is also when a weakly specified facility is most exposed. A guarantee may widen the volume a dealer can buy without absorbing the higher cost faced by farmers, the risk of late delivery or the effect of a poorer crop price. An appraisal must identify each risk and the party that remains responsible for it.

WHAT THREE PROGRAMMES SHOW

Kenya: test the link between transaction records and field use

AfDB describes an earlier Kenya project with Apollo Agriculture, approved in October 2023, comprising a US$2 million partial trade credit guarantee and a US$219,000 grant. The design combines finance, availability, extension, soil health and monitoring and aims to reach farmers through retail agro-dealers and village agents using a digital platform. Its planned distribution and reach are targets. This case is distinct from the newer Kenya approval reported in the AFFM annual summary. [1,4]

A digital transaction record offers a practical starting point: it can help follow approval, collection and repayment where those events are captured. It cannot establish when planting took place, which parcel received the fertiliser or whether the price was viable. A sample of independently checked farm transactions could link those pieces without making detailed monitoring a condition for every small purchase.

The unit tracked matters. An account may purchase for several plots; a dealer may allocate more than one input or extend different terms to different customers. A useful pilot therefore records the specific order, the farmer's actual net charge and the intended crop and season. It also samples people who were eligible but did not buy, including those who could not use the application or reach an outlet.

Tanzania: start with who gets stock and when

AfDB announced the launch of a distinct US$2 million trade credit guarantee project with the African Fertilizer and Agribusiness Partnership in September 2025. It presented a delivery ambition of 60,000 tonnes on credit. The announcement establishes the facility's purpose and intended scale; it does not demonstrate that deliveries reached that volume. [5]

AfDB's page for a separate, closed Tanzania project gives reported quantities and dealer reach, showing that channel data can be collected. However, its narrative and project header use different amounts for the earlier guarantee. This paper does not use the older project to calculate a comparative leverage ratio or infer the performance of the newer facility. [6]

A Tanzania pilot could prioritise dated stock arrivals and days without key products at the dealers expected to benefit. Link these records to the credit actually drawn and to comparable dealers facing similar demand. Interview retailers about credit days, stock diversity and late-payment consequences. If purchases move between dealers without improving timely access, increased sales at participating outlets could overstate the facility's contribution.

Sierra Leone: specify what the grant and guarantee buy separately

AfDB's Sierra Leone FOSTER project summary records approval on 6 October 2025. It describes a US$1.5 million partial trade credit guarantee and a US$700,000 technical assistance grant, with Welthungerhilfe as implementer. The project combines finance with policy work and soil health and extension services. Its 2028 reach and distribution figures are planned results. [7]

The two instruments should have separate accountabilities. The guarantee should be assessed on additional credit available on workable terms and the stock and sales it enables. Grant spending should be traced to services actually delivered, such as advice, demonstrations or field assessments. A large sales total cannot validate the grant; a large training total cannot validate the guarantee.

An early test is whether finance and advice reach the same communities in time for the same decision. A farmer can attend a session after planting or find that the advised product is unavailable locally. Neither activity is necessarily wasted, but the pairing intended by the project has not occurred that season. Link the two records before judging the combination.

CaseDelivery feature to testEvidence required to support expansion
Kenya, Apollo projectDigital transactions and local agents alongside extension.Confirm order terms, on-time access, field suitability and who is excluded from the channel.
Tanzania, 2025 launchSupplier trade credit intended to improve distribution.Compare seasonal stock availability, credit pass-through, prices and funded quantities.
Sierra Leone, FOSTERPartial guarantee paired with technical assistance and policy support.Verify use of each instrument and whether advice and suitable inputs reach the same farms in time.

Source: StoneComms interpretation of the three project designs [4,5,7]. The cases compare implementation choices rather than national performance.

AFFORDABILITY IS A SEASONAL CASH DECISION

A farm's cash requirement is affected by more than the price on a bag. The delivered bill can include transport, fees and interest; the value of incremental crop output depends on the price a farmer can obtain after harvest, alongside additional labour or marketing costs. A gain in yield need not translate into additional cash after debt service. The proposition also needs to survive a poor but plausible season.

The first distinction is between liquidity and total cost. A product may be commercially useful but unaffordable at the time of purchase. Deferred payment can address that timing problem while increasing total cost or transferring risk onto a household. If the underlying activity loses money under reasonable assumptions, longer credit does not repair it.

A field experiment reported by Duflo, Kremer and Robinson in western Kenya found that a small, time-limited offer with free delivery soon after harvest increased fertiliser purchases. It makes purchase timing a credible variable to test. The study was published in 2011 and does not establish responses to current prices, products or programmes. It also does not imply that every farmer who chooses not to buy is making a mistake. [8]

For a new facility, compare credit with alternatives that address the problem directly: a reservation with delivery before planting, a saving arrangement through a cooperative, or a different stocking schedule. Each is a hypothesis, not a substitute for local evidence. The cheapest effective intervention could be changing when the product is offered rather than expanding the balance sheet that carries it.

SOIL HEALTH CHANGES THE INVESTMENT TEST

The African Union's Fertilizer and Soil Health Action Plan covers markets and finance alongside integrated soil fertility management. Its framework brings mineral and organic approaches, water management and advice into the same policy picture. That matters because trade finance selects for goods that can be sold and repaid; it does not by itself select a field-level response that is agronomically suitable. [9]

The investment question is whether the financed offer allows farmers to act on credible advice. Before expanding a facility, ask who pays for advice, whether the adviser has incentives tied to volume, and what farmers can do when the recommended product or practice is unavailable or unaffordable. Practical advice should recognise where water, labour or another input is the binding constraint.

Soil tests and training sessions are service counts. They do not establish that advice was implemented, or that soil health changed. For a credible evaluation, document baseline conditions, compare practice with a suitable reference and follow outcomes beyond a single delivery season. Environmental questions such as inefficient nutrient use or losses to water should remain visible alongside possible yield benefits.

THE TWO-LEDGER APPRAISAL

  • Define the claim the facility is making and the counterfactual against which it will be judged.
  • Reconcile channel and farm observations for the same crop, catchment and season.
  • Keep stock, farm returns, repayment and environmental outcomes separate in the approval decision.

StoneComms original synthesis: Programme documents establish different financed activities, while the western Kenya study illustrates the possible significance of timing and the African Union plan establishes the relevance of soil management. The analytical bridge is that sales can expand without resolving the constraints that determine successful farm use. A matched two-ledger approach can locate these breaks. This is a proposed appraisal framework; it has not been applied to participant records for the three cases. [4,5,7–9]

Channel ledger

Start with ordinary credit terms and document which obligations the guarantee changes: eligible counterparties, cash deposit, credit days, rates, limits and the treatment of arrears. Track actual drawdowns and seasonal receipts rather than counting an approved limit as credit deployed. Connect each sampled delivery to a dated order, and record stockouts or substitutions. Request losses, recoveries and guarantee claims in addition to sales.

Farm ledger

For a consented sample, record payment terms, transaction fees, collection travel, actual delivery before or after the planting decision, and the advice received. Compare expected crop receipts with the full costs and later record observed results, including the repayment source if available. Repayment from off-farm income may be financially sound for the lender without establishing the crop economics that justified the facility.

Reconciliation and decision

Review a financed cohort and an appropriate comparison group at the same point in the season. If credit draws rise but deliveries remain late, investigate stock planning before increasing cover. If deliveries improve but farm margins do not, examine product choice, terms and prices. If both improve but losses threaten sustainability, revisit the allocation of risk rather than assuming a broader guarantee is the answer.

Use shared definitions across markets, but set the thresholds locally. Planting calendars, distribution distances, public support and delivery models differ. More credit in a reasonably supplied market and first access in a remote district are different achievements; the same sales metric can obscure both.

IMPLICATIONS AND COMMISSIONABLE RESEARCH

For guarantors, make the risk being underwritten explicit and establish how the improved credit terms will be shown to reach dealers or farmers. Ask for funded sales, timely delivery, recoveries and evidence of additional activity relative to credible alternatives. Separate the lender's exposure from household debt and delivery risks when considering an extension.

For public agencies and implementers, budget separately for extension and verification so that neither is dependent on the volume sold. Ask which farmers are missed and why. Relevant differences may include tenancy, distance, access to a phone, cash timing and the power to decide what is grown or purchased. Participation counts cannot reveal the effect of those constraints on household decisions.

A commissionable study could trace two planting seasons in selected Kenya and Tanzania catchments and build a delivery baseline for Sierra Leone. It would reconcile dealer credit and inventory records with a consented farm panel and independently verified delivery windows. Compare actual prices and terms with realistic alternatives, interview non-participants and gather field-specific agronomic evidence. Define missing-data and consent procedures before collection, and use an independent evaluator for decisions on continuation.

The practical output would be a market-by-market decision on which element to extend, redesign or stop. Report the evidence separately for additional finance, timely access, farm margins, repayment and soil-related outcomes. Identify who pays for each next step and which result would overturn the expansion recommendation.

COMMUNITIES AND THE UN SDGS

SDG 2, Zero Hunger, is the primary classification because smallholder productivity and access to appropriate farm inputs are the paper's central concerns. SDG 12, Responsible Consumption and Production, applies because the suitability and efficient use of those inputs are central to the research question. Affordability Is a Seasonal Cash Decision and Soil Health Changes the Investment Test explain those classifications.

The people affected include smallholder farmers, household members exposed to debt, retail staff and advisers. Wider risks include exclusion of less connected farmers and nutrient losses where inputs are poorly matched. No farmer or community interviews were undertaken. Before claiming benefits, measure timely use, net farm returns, distribution of access and debt risk, and site-specific nutrient performance separately.

Goals 1, 5, 8 and 10 have conditional links through household income, access and retail livelihoods; goals 6, 13 and 15 relate to potential environmental trade-offs. Goals 9, 16 and 17 are secondary through distribution systems, accountability and institutional cooperation. The evidence does not establish a distinct relationship with goals 3, 4, 7, 11 or 14. The chart shows editorial relevance only, not measured impact or United Nations endorsement.

CONCLUSION

A trade credit guarantee can strengthen the distribution channel that connects farmers to inputs. Its value should be judged against where access was constrained, who actually got better terms, and what the purchased input made possible. The case for a larger facility is strongest when independent channel and farm records tell the same story.

The question worth asking before expansion is whether the next funded purchase can be made in time, can be used appropriately and makes economic sense for the farm taking the risk. If the answer is unclear, additional evidence may be more valuable than additional guarantee capacity.
fieldData.methodology:
METHODOLOGY

Comparative public-source desk research completed on 26 November 2026. The unit of comparison is the proposed mechanism linking trade credit to a farm decision, not national fertiliser consumption or performance. Kenya, Tanzania and Sierra Leone were selected because the public project records describe complementary approaches to distribution and support. Programme reports establish institutional claims, designs and reported activity; they are distinct from independent findings.

The research compares the obligations and measurement points across cases. The original two-ledger appraisal draws on those project designs, an earlier western Kenya experiment and the African Union's policy framework. The research does not extrapolate a treatment effect, calculate a guarantee leverage rate or model investment returns.
fieldData.limitations:
LIMITATIONS

The public documents do not provide aligned seasonal transactions, executed guarantee terms, participant cash flows, non-participant observations or comparable agronomic outcomes. Approvals and targets do not establish delivery. The older Tanzania programme is separate from the 2025 launch; inconsistent guarantee amounts on its public project page are a reason not to compare leverage figures.

Reported portfolio sales and volumes do not establish additionality. The global price index does not describe local selling prices, and a historical experiment cannot determine how current markets respond. No original fieldwork, independent audit, soil testing or commercial valuation was undertaken. This research does not provide agronomic prescriptions or investment advice.

fieldData.seo-title: Fertiliser Finance in Africa: Trade Credit and Farm Affordability
fieldData.seo-description: A comparison of Kenya, Tanzania and Sierra Leone tests how fertiliser guarantees can support timely farm access, affordability and responsible nutrient use.
fieldData.sdg-rationale: SDG 2 is primary: suitable, timely farm inputs and their use by smallholders are central. SDG 12: appropriate input selection and responsible nutrient use are part of the appraisal. Editorial relevance, not measured impact or UN endorsement.
